primaryKeyword: seo for agriculture companies in india
secondaryKeywords: tractor and implement brand search visibility
h1: SEO for agri-input, farm machinery and agritech brands
metaTitle: SEO for Agriculture Companies in India
metaDescription: The one Indian vertical where the answer engine is YouTube and the query is spoken, not typed. English-first here is malpractice, not a preference.
answer: In agriculture the buyer speaks the query rather than typing it, and the answer usually sits on YouTube. So the working unit is a video whose full transcript is published as a page on your own domain, in the language the question was asked in. The first winnable queries are price and dealer, not brand.
takeaways: Your competitor on **[model] price** is an aggregator with a page for every model in every state — not the rival manufacturer. It wins on page count and freshness, not on knowing the machine.
A video that lives only on YouTube builds YouTube's asset. Embedded on your page with the **full transcript as text**, it builds yours too.
Machine-translating the English site into Hindi is worse than publishing nothing. The same implement has three regional names and none is the dictionary word.
Publish six to eight weeks **before** the sowing window. By the time the tractor is in the field, the decision is two months old.
One indexable URL per dealer. A pin on a map is not a page, and Google cannot rank a pin.

sections.h2: The query is spoken, and it is rarely in English
body: Picture the actual search. A farmer in Beed or Bathinda holds up the phone, taps the microphone, and asks a full sentence — which wheat variety for late sowing, why the cotton leaves are curling, what a 45 HP tractor costs on road. That reaches Google as a long string, sometimes in Devanagari, more often in Latin letters typed by whoever in the family is better with a keyboard.

Almost none of that shows up in an English keyword tool. Volume for a transliterated phrase splits across a dozen spellings and gets reported as zero, so a plan built from an exported spreadsheet chases demand that isn't there and misses the demand that is. Here, keyword research starts with the sales team, the dealer WhatsApp groups and your own YouTube comments, and only then goes to a tool.
What that does to page structure is specific, and it is not a translation project.
bullets: **One URL per language**, declared with [hreflang](/glossary/hreflang). A toggle that swaps text at the same URL gives Google one page, and it picks one language to rank.
**Headings written as the spoken question.** If people ask it in nine words, the H2 is nine words long.

**A two-line direct answer under each heading**, before the explanation. Spoken queries pull short answers into snippets and AI summaries, and a page that buries the answer in paragraph four loses both.
**Numerals, not words.** People type 45 HP, not forty-five horsepower.
**Regional term variants in the body copy.** A rotavator, a cultivator and a seed drill each go by different names across states, and the state your buyer is in decides which one they said out loud.

callout.title: Do not machine-translate the English site
callout.body: A translated page reaches for the dictionary word for an implement or a pest, and the dictionary word is not the word farmers use. You get a page nobody searches for, sitting alongside an English page that was working, splitting whatever signal you had. Have the vernacular pages written by someone who has sold in that state. Longer take in [SEO in Hindi and Indian languages](/journal/seo-in-hindi-and-indian-languages).

sections.h2: YouTube is the answer surface, and your site is where the transcript lives
body: For most agri questions the first useful result is a video, and the research happens there — a demo in a field, a review by someone who owns the machine, a comparison shot from the driver's seat. That isn't a preference to argue with. It's what a person does when reading is slower than watching.

Two mistakes follow. Publishing only on YouTube builds an audience on a platform that doesn't send you the enquiry. Embedding the video on a page carrying eighty words of copy gives search nothing to read and nothing to rank.

The transcript-backed page fixes both, and it's the most useful content unit in this industry, because it turns spoken content — the thing your dealers and agronomists are already good at producing — into indexable text without asking anyone to write an essay. It's also how Google wants video handled: the [watch page hosting the video has to be indexed and performing in Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/video) before the video itself is considered, so a bare embed on a thin page fails twice over.
numbered: **Upload a transcript file to YouTube** rather than relying on automatic captions, which are generated in one language and are unreliable on field audio.
**Build the page on your domain**: embed at the top, then the full transcript as readable text, broken by subheadings that match the questions it answers.
**Add the numbers the video mentions but doesn't show** — HP band, implement compatibility, tyre size, fuel tank, warranty, service interval.
**Add the commercial line**: price band, nearest dealer, book a demo. On a phone that means a call button and a WhatsApp link, not a form.
**One page per crop and per implement**, not a single page called Videos with thirty embeds on it. That page ranks for nothing, and it's why most brands conclude video doesn't work for search.

callout.title: The transcript is not duplicate content
callout.body: A transcript on your site and captions on YouTube are two pages on two domains, and the video is one asset appearing in both places by design. What would be duplication is the same transcript pasted across ten near-identical model pages. Our [YouTube SEO work](/services/youtube-seo-services) treats the channel and the site as one asset with two shelves.

sections.h2: The price query you handed to an aggregator
body: Search any tractor model with the word price after it. Count how far down you get before a manufacturer appears. On most models you don't get there at all — the slots belong to marketplaces and content sites that have built a page for every model, every variant and every state, and that keep them refreshed.

Brands cede this deliberately, usually out of legal nervousness: the dealer sets the on-road number, so publishing a price feels like a commitment you can't keep. That's a real constraint and a bad excuse. The searcher isn't asking you to sign a quotation. They're asking whether this machine is in their range at all, and they'll get the answer from a site that has never seen it.

Publish what you can defend. Ex-showroom range by variant with a visible as-of date; the components that make up the on-road number — registration, insurance, accessories, dealer charges — explained so the gap stops feeling like a trick; what changes it by state; then a dealer link for the exact figure. That page becomes the only authoritative one in the result set, a position no aggregator can buy.

Comparison queries work the same way. Brands won't write **[model A] vs [model B]** because it means naming a rival. Write the ones where you win on a dimension you can state — lift capacity, fuel use per hour, service network density — and say plainly where you don't. Readers know you're not neutral. What they're testing is whether you're honest.
bullets: **Agritech apps have the same problem in reverse.** Nobody searches your app name. They search the problem it solves, and a content farm is answering.

**Crop-protection claims are regulated.** Keep product pages to what's on the approved label and route the rest to agronomy content that makes no efficacy claim. It's the one place here where a keen writer creates a compliance problem rather than a ranking one.

**Input brands are searched by active ingredient**, not only by brand name, because that's what the label, the dealer and the agri officer all use. Pages carrying only brand names are invisible to half the demand.

sections.h2: One page per dealer, named the way a farmer says it
body: Most dealer locators here are a state dropdown, a district dropdown and a map. There's nothing for Google to index, so the brand ranks for its own name and nothing else, while directories collect every **[brand] dealer in [town]** search in the country.
Give every dealer a real URL. Once the template exists it costs almost nothing, and it's the fastest measurable win available to a brand that sells through a network.
bullets: **Name it the way it's searched.** Brand, dealer name, and the tehsil or nearest large town — the village name has no volume and the tehsil does. Mention both in the body anyway.
**Address in both scripts**, phone as a click-to-call link, a WhatsApp link, and opening hours including the local market day.

**What the dealer stocks** — models, implements, whether spares and service are on site, whether they run demos, which finance tie-ups they hold. That last one decides more tractor sales than any brochure page.

**LocalBusiness structured data on each page**, so address, hours and phone are machine-readable rather than baked into an image. See [schema markup](/glossary/schema-markup) if that's new to your developer.
**A district or state index page above them**, linking down. Without it the dealer pages are orphans and get crawled once.

callout.title: Don't create Business Profiles for dealers you don't own
callout.body: Google's guidelines are explicit that each location gets one profile and duplicates aren't allowed. A brand team creating profiles on a network's behalf usually produces duplicates, an ownership fight, and a suspension the dealer has to clean up. Help them claim and fix theirs instead, and keep the page on your domain as the asset you control. Mechanics in [tier-2 local SEO](/journal/local-seo-in-tier-2-india).

sections.h2: The publishing calendar is the crop calendar
body: Agriculture has the most predictable demand curve of any industry we work in, and almost nobody publishes against it. Content ships when the content calendar says so — which means when the marketing team has bandwidth, which is roughly the opposite of when the farmer is deciding.
The rule: a page has to be published, indexed and gathering impressions before the decision window opens, and that takes weeks. So you publish six to eight weeks ahead of the season, not during it.

bullets: **Refresh rather than republish.** A wheat variety page rewritten each August with the current advisory keeps its history. A new URL every year throws it away.
**Machinery demand follows the harvest, not the sowing.** People buy equipment when money has arrived. Time the finance and offer pages to that.

sections.h2: Subsidy portals open, and the demand arrives that week
body: Farm machinery subsidy is administered through the central Digital Platform for Farm Mechanization and Technology, run by the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, and through the state agriculture department portals under it. When a state opens an application window, search for that scheme goes near-vertical for a few days and then falls away.

Most marketing teams never plan for that shape, because it doesn't look like a campaign. It looks like a page that has to already be there. Write one page per scheme you're genuinely relevant to, and give each an owner and a review date — these rules change, and a stale subsidy page is a customer signing on the strength of a number you no longer honour.

Each page carries what the scheme covers, who's eligible, the documents needed, the sequence of steps, where it typically stalls, and which of your models are on the approved list. Then a date at the top and a link to the government portal, so the reader can verify you rather than trust you.

callout.title: Never imply you can get a subsidy approved
callout.body: You can explain the scheme, prepare the paperwork and confirm which of your machines are listed. You cannot approve an application, and a page that blurs that line will produce angry phone calls in the same week it produces enquiries. State the boundary on the page. It costs you nothing and it is the difference between a trusted brand page and a lead-bait page.

sections.h2: What we'd do first, and what we commit to
body: For an agri brand with an English brochure site and a YouTube channel, month one is not brand content. It's a dealer URL per outlet with index pages above them, one honest price page per model family, and transcript-backed pages built from the ten videos you've already paid to make. All three are recoverable ground rather than new ground, which is why they move first. Then the seasonal layer, planned backwards from the sowing windows, in the two or three languages your sales map justifies — not eleven.

Most of this converts on a call or a WhatsApp message rather than a form, which breaks default analytics. Fix the measurement before you scale the content, or you'll be arguing about attribution in month four. [Tracking WhatsApp and phone leads](/answers/how-to-track-whatsapp-and-phone-leads-in-ga4) is the place to start.

Our SEO runs from ₹75,000/mo, and from ₹40,000/mo for smaller sites. Ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, 30 days' notice, and you keep every asset — dealer templates, transcripts, schema, all of it. Numbers on [our pricing page](/pricing). We don't promise a ranking position: we freeze your trailing-90-day qualified enquiries from organic search on day one, and if we haven't beaten that number in 90 days we keep working free until we do.

faqs.q: Should we publish in English or in Hindi first?
faqs.a: In the language your buyers speak, which for machinery and inputs is usually not English. Keep English for distributors, investors and export enquiries. If budget forces a choice, take the two or three state languages that cover most of your sales map and do them properly, rather than covering ten badly.

faqs.q: Do farmers actually search Google, or is it all YouTube and WhatsApp?
faqs.a: All three, in sequence. The question usually starts as a spoken Google search, the answer is often a video, and the decision gets argued out on WhatsApp with a dealer or a neighbour. That's why the transcript-backed page matters: it sits in the Google result, plays in the YouTube result, and forwards as a link.

faqs.q: Can we publish prices if the dealer sets the on-road figure?
faqs.a: Yes, if you publish the right number. An ex-showroom range by variant with an as-of date and an explanation of what registration, insurance and accessories add is defensible and useful. Refusing to publish anything doesn't protect you — it just means an aggregator's estimate is the number your buyer sees.

faqs.q: We're an agritech app, not a machinery brand. Does any of this apply?
faqs.a: The surfaces are identical; the content unit changes. Nobody searches for your app by name, so you compete on the problem it solves — a symptom, a rate, a scheme, a calculation. Your competitor is a content site with no product, and you beat it by being the page that answers the question and then does the thing.

faqs.q: How long before this shows results?
faqs.a: Dealer and price pages often show impressions inside eight to twelve weeks because competition on those precise queries is thin. Seasonal content is judged a season later by definition — a Rabi page published in August is assessed in December. Plan the first review for 90 days and the real read for two seasons.
